blocks.text: [II, 747] Because many ancient writers did not pay sufficient attention to these points, they invented a great deal about the ἀνακαίνωσις [anakainōsis] and ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of eagles, which it is tedious to report here ^{(5)}. Well known is the fiction of Saadia, cited by Kimchi on Psal. CIII. and Es. XL.: הנשר יעוף על כל העופות ויעלה מאד על פני רקיע השמים ויקרוב לחום האש היסודי ויפול עצמו בים מרוב חום ויתחדש ויעלה אבר וישוב לימי עלומיו כן כל עשר עד מאה וכשיגיע למאה יעלה כמנהגו ויפול בים וימות שם, The eagle flies higher than any of the birds and is carried far up towards the firmament, until it comes near the elemental fire. Then, burning with the heat, it throws itself headlong into the sea, and is renewed; its feathers grow again, and it returns to the days of its youth. And this happens every ten years up to the hundredth year; when it has reached that, it is carried upward as usual, falls headlong into the sea, and dies there. Similar is what we read in Porta coeli fol. 22, col. 2: ויש אומרים כי הנשר טבעו לעלות קרוב לגבול האש ומתלהב בסוף עשר שנים לעשר שנים ומרוב חמומו מפיל עצמו בים לקרר חומו ושם ימרט נוצתו ויתחדש נוצה אחרת ויתחדש כחו עד ק׳ שנה שיעלה שם ויפול בים ויטבע, There are some who say that it is natural to the eagle to ascend close to the boundary of fire and to be set ablaze every ten years, and, burning with the heat, to cast itself into the sea to cool that heat; and that there its feathers fall out and others grow in their place, and its strength is restored, up to the hundredth year, when, carried up to the same place, it falls headlong and is drowned in the sea. Others say it is plunged not into the sea but into a spring, and, washed in it, grows young again. Damir, on العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] alokab, that is, περὶ τοῦ μελαναιέτου [peri tou melanaietou] [on the black eagle], which is a kind of eagle especially common in Arabia Felix: متي ثقلت عن النهوض او عميت حملتها الفراخ ونقلتها من مكان الي مكان تلتمس لها عينا صافيتا بارض الهند علي راس جبل فيتغمسها فيها ثم تضعها في شعاع الشمس فيذهب ريشها وينبت لها ريش جديد ويذهب ظلمة بصرها ثم تعوص في تلك العين [matā thaqulat ʿan al-nuhūḍ aw ʿamiyat ḥamalathā al-firākh wa-naqalathā min makān ilā makān taltamisu lahā ʿaynan ṣāfiyatan bi-arḍ al-Hind ʿalā raʾs jabal fa-yataghammasuhā fīhā thumma taḍaʿuhā fī shuʿāʿ al-shams fa-yadhhabu rīshuhā wa-yanbutu lahā rīsh jadīd wa-yadhhabu ẓulmat baṣarihā thumma taʿūṣu fī tilka al-ʿayn] [col. 168] فاذا هي قد عادت شابة [fa-idhā hiya qad ʿādat shābba] And when it becomes slow in flight and goes blind, its chicks carry it and move it from place to place, and in India they seek for it a pure spring on the summit of a mountain; they plunge it into this and set it facing the rays of the sun. Then its feathers fall out and new ones grow for it, and the dimness of its eyes is dispelled; and it is plunged [II, 748] again into the same spring, when its grey age has returned. The author of the Letter to Praesidius, which is attributed to Jerome: When the eagle has grown old, its feathers and eyes become heavy; it seeks a spring, raises its feathers, and gathers heat into itself, and so its eyes are healed; and it plunges itself three times into the spring, and thus returns to youth. Eustathius, on the Hexaëmeron, p. 27: Φασὶ γηράσαντα τὸν ἀετὸν ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ὄψεις, καὶ βαρεῖσθαι αὐτοῦ τὰς πτέρυγας, καὶ εἰς πηγὴν ἀφικνεῖσθαι, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰθέρα ἀνιπτάμενον, ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τὰς πτέρυγας καταφλέγεσθαι, καὶ ἀναβλέπειν· εἶθ᾽ εὐθὺς ἐπὶ τὴν πηγὴν καταβάντα τρίτον βαπτίζεσθαι, καὶ ἀνανεοῦσθαι. Διὸ καὶ τὸν Ψαλμὸν φάσκειν φησὶν, Ἀνακαινισθήσεται ὡς ἀετοῦ ἡ νεότης σου. [Phasi gērasanta ton aeton amaurousthai tas opseis, kai bareisthai autou tas pterygas, kai eis pēgēn aphikneisthai, kai eis ton aithera aniptamenon, hypo tou hēliou tas pterygas kataphlegesthai, kai anablepein; eith᾽ euthys epi tēn pēgēn katabanta triton baptizesthai, kai ananeousthai. Dio kai ton Psalmon phaskein phēsin, Anakainisthēsetai hōs aetou hē neotēs sou.] They say that the eagle, worn out by old age, has the sharpness of its eyes dulled and its wings grow heavy, and it makes for a spring; and while it is carried up in flight into the air, its wings are scorched by the sun and it recovers its sight; then, when it comes down into the spring, it is plunged into it three times and renewed. And therefore the Psalm said, „Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's“. An Anonymous writer on the Psalms: Ὁ ἀετὸς κατὰ φ´ ἔτη ἀνακαινίζεται. καιόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, καὶ καταδυόμενος εἰς πηγὴν ὕδατος, πάλιν νέος εὑρίσκεται. [Ho aetos kata ph´ etē anakainizetai. kaiomenos hypo tou hēliou, kai katadyomenos eis pēgēn hydatos, palin neos heurisketai.] The eagle is renewed every five hundredth year. Scorched by the sun and plunged into a spring of water, it is found young again. Some write ϱ´ [r´], that is, hundredth, instead of φ´ [ph´], that is, five hundredth, so that this writer may agree with Epiphanius, whose words are: Ἀετὸς δὲ καλεῖται διὰ τὴν πολυετίαν αὐτοῦ. οὗτος μὲν ζῇ ἔτη ἑκατὸν, καὶ γηράσαντος γρυποῦται ὁ προμυκτὴρ, καὶ ἀμβλυώττουσιν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ μὴ ὁρᾷν, καὶ οὐκ ἰσχύει φαγεῖν. ἀνέρχεται δὲ εἰς ὕψος λίαν, καὶ ῥίπτει ἑαυτὸν ἐπὶ ἀκροτόμου πέτρας, προσκρούσας αὐτῇ τὸ ῥάμφος, καὶ λούεται ἐπὶ τὴν ψυγρὰν λίμνην, καὶ κάθηται κατὰ τὸ ἡλιακὸν θερμὸν, πίπτουσι δὲ λεπίδες ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, καὶ πάλιν εἰς νέους τελεῖν ἄρχεται. [Aetos de kaleitai dia tēn polyetian autou. houtos men zē etē hekaton, kai gērasantos gryproutai ho promyktēr, kai amblyōttousin hoi ophthalmoi autou, tou mē horan, kai ouk ischyei phagein. anerchetai de eis hypsos lian, kai rhiptei heauton epi akrotomou petras, proskrousas autē to rhamphos, kai louetai epi tēn psygran limnēn, kai kathētai kata to hēliakon thermon, piptousi de lepides apo tōn ophthalmōn, kai palin eis neous telein archetai.] The eagle is called ἀετὸς [aetos] on account of its long life. For it lives a hundred years. But when it grows old, its beak becomes hooked and its eyes grow dim, so that it can neither see nor eat. So it rises on high and hurls itself against a sheer rock, against which it strikes its beak; and it washes itself in a cold lake and sits in the heat of the sun; and scales fall from its eyes, and it grows young again. Augustine too, on Psalm 102, writes that the upper beak of an ageing eagle grows so much that the passage for eating is closed. This very thing Aristotle ^{a)}, Pliny ^{b)} and Horapollo ^{c)} expressly teach. But whereas they add that with its beak growing in this way it dies of hunger, Augustine asserts that, having worn down its beak against a rock, it restores its failing strength by eating. Yet lest anyone think this is handed down by him as certain, here are the holy man's words on Psalm LXVI.: Our youth shall be renewed like the eagle, provided only that we wear down our old age against the rock. Whether those things are true, etc., which are said about the eagle, [II, 749] or whether it is rather a report of men than the truth, yet the truth is in the Scriptures, and not without reason have the Scriptures said this. Let us do whatever it signifies, and not trouble ourselves how true it is. Indeed, since the things that the writers we have cited relate about the ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of the eagle are either false or uncertain, let us embrace only what all acknowledge as true and certain: namely, that the eagle at a fixed time casts off its old feathers and then takes on others, and is renewed in this way. Hence the genuine Jerome, on Isaiah chapter 40: We have often said that the old age of eagles grows young again by the changing of their feathers. And Euthymius on Psalm CII.: You will lay aside the feeble old age which diseases and sins had brought on, ὡς ἐκεῖνος τὸ γῆρας τῶν ἑαυτοῦ πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos to gēras tōn heautou pterōn], [col. 169] as it does the old age of its feathers. You will be renewed through repentance, ὡς ἐκεῖνος διὰ τῆς παλιφυΐας πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos dia tēs paliphyias pterōn], as it is through the regrowth of its feathers.
